paragraph: Maytas Infra (India), news of 16-17 December 2008. Maytas Infra builds roads, irrigation and metro projects. It is controlled by the Raju family, who also founded Satyam Computer Services. On the evening of 16 December, Satyam's board approved buying Maytas Infra and the unlisted Maytas Properties for about US$1.6 billion. Investors objected that cash was being moved to the founders' family firms, and the deal was withdrawn before the market opened on 17 December. Rivals: other listed construction contractors (L&T, Jaiprakash Associates, Punj Lloyd, IVRCL, HCC, Nagarjuna Construction, Gammon, Patel Engineering).

Thinksoft Global (India), 16 February 2010. Thinksoft tests banking software for banks and insurers. It listed in October 2009 and its price had risen steeply. In mid-February the exchanges moved the stock into the trade-for-trade surveillance segment, and it hit lower price limits on 16 and 17 February. Rivals: the 10 largest listed IT services firms (TCS, Wipro, Mphasis, HCL Tech, Rolta, Tech Mahindra, Oracle Financial Services, Polaris, Patni, 3i Infotech).

Core Education & Technologies (India), 25 February 2013. Core sells IT-based education services to schools and governments. On 25 February, reports said lenders were selling Core shares that an investor had pledged and could not top up. Panic selling followed (about -60% that day), and SEBI opened a probe into the selling in several small and mid caps. Rivals: other listed education-services firms (Educomp, Everonn, Aptech).

Sudar Industries (India), 25 February 2013. A garment exporter, named in the same 25 February selling of pledged shares in several small and mid caps. Rivals: listed textile and garment firms (Raymond, Arvind, Alok, Bombay Dyeing, S. Kumars).

Aanjaneya Lifecare, later Dr Datsons Labs (India), 25 February 2013. A pharmaceutical maker, named in the same 25 February selling of pledged shares; it fell about 56% in six sessions. Rivals: the 10 largest listed pharmaceutical firms.

Gitanjali Gems (India), 14 February 2018. A jewellery maker and retailer controlled by Mehul Choksi. On 14 February, Punjab National Bank disclosed a Rs 11,400 crore fraud through letters of undertaking issued for firms of Nirav Modi and of Choksi's Gitanjali group, and enforcement raids followed. Rivals: other listed jewellers (PC Jeweller, Titan, Rajesh Exports).

Reliance Communications (India), 4 February 2019. A telecom firm of the Anil Ambani (ADAG) group that had shut most mobile services in 2017-18. On 4 February its board said 18 months of asset sales had failed to repay lenders (debt above Rs 46,000 crore) and that it would go to the insolvency tribunal. Rivals: other telecom operators (Bharti Airtel, Vodafone Idea, Tata Communications).

Reliance Capital (India), 12 June 2019. The ADAG group's NBFC holding company (lending, insurance, mutual fund, broking), funded by bank loans, bonds and commercial paper. On the evening of 11 June its auditor PwC resigned, saying its queries had not been answered satisfactorily; the company called the observations baseless. The group was under debt stress. No missed payment, default or rating cut by Reliance Capital was reported on that day. Rivals: the 10 largest listed NBFCs and housing-finance companies (including Indiabulls Housing, Bajaj Finance, DHFL, LIC Housing).

CG Power (India), 20 August 2019. A maker of transformers, switchgear and motors (formerly Crompton Greaves) in the Avantha group. On 20 August it disclosed that an internal review had found unauthorised transactions hiding about Rs 635 crore of liabilities. Rivals: other electrical-equipment makers (BHEL, Siemens, ABB).

Indiabulls Housing Finance (India), 6 September 2019. A housing-finance company funded by bank loans, bonds, commercial paper and debt mutual funds. On 6 September, reports of a public-interest petition alleging that the promoters diverted funds through shell companies hit the stock. The company denied the claims; the Delhi High Court listed the petition for later in the month. No missed payment was reported. Rivals: other housing-finance companies (HDFC, DHFL, LIC Housing, PNB Housing, Can Fin, Aavas, Repco).

Future Retail (India), 6 March 2020. The Big Bazaar supermarket chain of the Future group. On 6 March a disclosure showed promoter shares pledged for debentures of a group entity, and lower price limits followed from 13 March. The COVID crash and lockdown fall within the next month. Rivals: other listed retailers (DMart, Trent, Aditya Birla Fashion).

Omaxe (India), 29 June 2020. A North-India property developer with 52% of promoter shares pledged. On 29 June it postponed the board meeting for its annual results by a month, and the stock hit lower limits for two days. Rivals: other listed developers (DLF, Godrej Properties, Oberoi Realty, Prestige).

Xerox (US), 3 October 2000. A copier maker. On 3 October it gave its fourth profit warning in five quarters, blaming its own sales and billing problems. It then cut the dividend and said it could not borrow in the commercial-paper market, while denying bankruptcy rumours. Rivals: S&P 500 firms in its sub-industry (HP, NetApp, Western Digital).

Xcel Energy (US), 26 July 2002. A utility holding company that owned NRG Energy, a merchant power producer. On 26 July, S&P cut NRG to junk, triggering about $1.1-1.3 billion of collateral demands, and Moody's put Xcel under review because it might have to support NRG. Context: the 2002 merchant-energy credit squeeze after Enron. Rivals: 11 S&P 500 multi-utilities.

Citigroup (US), 19 November 2008. The largest US bank by assets, funded by deposits (much of them uninsured and foreign), wholesale debt and repo. On 19 November it said it would take the remaining $17.4 billion of assets of its structured investment vehicles onto its balance sheet, deepening doubts about its capital. Rivals: other large S&P 500 banks (BofA, JPMorgan, PNC, Truist, US Bancorp, Wells Fargo).

Hartford Financial (US), 30 October 2008. A property-casualty and life insurer. It reported a $2.6 billion third-quarter loss on investments and halved its 2008 guidance; analysts said it might need $2 billion of capital. Rivals: S&P 500 property-casualty insurers (Allstate, Cincinnati Financial, Progressive, Travelers).

Cigna (US), 30 October 2008. A health insurer. Third-quarter profit fell 53% on losses in its run-off variable-annuity reinsurance business, and it cut its outlook. Rivals: S&P 500 firms in its current sub-industry, Health Care Services (CVS, DaVita, LabCorp, Quest).

Bank of America (US), 16 January 2009. It reported a fourth-quarter loss, mostly from Merrill Lynch. The government announced a second capital injection of $20 billion and a guarantee on about $118 billion of assets. Rivals: other large S&P 500 banks (Citi, JPMorgan, PNC, Truist, US Bancorp, Wells Fargo).

State Street (US), 20 January 2009. A custody bank funded mostly by large clients' uninsured deposits and wholesale money. Fourth-quarter profit fell 71%, and investors feared it would need capital after moving troubled conduit assets onto its balance sheet. 20 January was also a broad bank sell-off day. Rivals: S&P 500 firms in its sub-industry, mostly asset managers (Ameriprise, Franklin, Invesco, Northern Trust, T. Rowe Price).

Regions Financial (US), 20 January 2009. A regional bank. Its fourth-quarter net loss was $6.2 billion, mostly a $6.0 billion non-cash goodwill write-down, plus a $1.15 billion loan-loss provision. 20 January was also a broad bank sell-off day. Rivals: other S&P 500 regional banks (Fifth Third, Huntington, KeyCorp, M&T).

Fifth Third (US), 22 January 2009. A regional bank. Fourth-quarter loss of $2.2 billion from a goodwill write-down and higher loan-loss reserves. Rivals: other S&P 500 regional banks (Huntington, KeyCorp, M&T, Regions).

Aflac (US), 22 January 2009. A supplemental insurer. A Morgan Stanley note questioned its capital, given $7.9 billion of hybrid securities (mostly bank preferreds). Aflac replied that its capital ratio was 425-475%, and its rating was cut one notch to AA-. Rivals: S&P 500 life and health insurers (Torchmark, MetLife, Principal, Prudential).

Textron (US), 29 January 2009. An aircraft (Cessna, Bell) and industrial group whose finance arm was being wound down. Fourth-quarter results showed write-downs at Textron Financial, a $625 million capital injection into it, job cuts and loss guidance. Rivals: S&P 500 aerospace and defence firms (Boeing, GE, General Dynamics, L3Harris, Lockheed, Northrop, RTX).

EPAM Systems (US), 24 February 2022. Software-engineering services with a large share of its engineers in Ukraine, Belarus and Russia. Russia's invasion of Ukraine on 24 February put its delivery centres at risk. Rivals: S&P 500 IT consulting firms (Accenture, Cognizant, Gartner, IBM).

Globe Life (US), 11 April 2024. A life and supplemental-health insurer. A short seller (Fuzzy Panda) alleged misconduct in its American Income Life agency force. Rivals: S&P 500 life and health insurers (Aflac, MetLife, Principal, Prudential).

Super Micro Computer (US), 30 October 2024. A server maker for AI data centres. Its auditor, Ernst & Young, resigned, saying it could no longer rely on management's representations, after a short-seller report and a delayed annual filing. Rivals: S&P 500 technology-hardware firms (Apple, Dell, HPE, HP, NetApp, Seagate, Western Digital).

Atlanta Ltd (India), 23 February 2007. A road and infrastructure builder. On 22 February, SEBI issued an interim order barring the company and its promoters from dealing in the shares and opened an investigation into the price rise and promoter buying. Rivals: other listed construction firms (IVRCL, L&T, Jaiprakash, Nagarjuna, Gammon, Patel, Simplex).

Wockhardt (India), 27 May 2014. A generic drug maker. Its results, released after the close on 26 May, showed profit down about 78% because US FDA import bans on several of its plants cut US sales, and fresh FDA concerns about another plant followed. Rivals: the 10 largest listed pharmaceutical firms.

Amtek Auto (India), 19 August 2015. A heavily indebted maker of forgings and castings. NSE said on 18 August that it would drop the stock from the derivatives segment, after a quarterly loss. Rivals: other listed auto-component makers (Bharat Forge, Bosch, Exide).

Reliance Power (India), 4 February 2019. An ADAG-group power producer. After Reliance Communications announced it would go to the insolvency tribunal, lenders to the promoter group sold pledged shares of group companies. Reliance Power itself was not reported to have missed a payment. Rivals: other listed power producers (NTPC, Adani Power, Tata Power, Torrent Power, CESC, NHPC).

Reliance Infrastructure (India), 4 February 2019. An ADAG-group EPC, roads and Delhi power-distribution company, hit by the same sales of pledged promoter-group shares. Rivals: listed construction and power firms (L&T, NCC, Tata Power, Torrent, CESC, IRB, Jaiprakash, HCC, KEC, Adani Energy Solutions).

Lakshmi Vilas Bank (India), 30 September 2019. A small private bank funded mainly by retail deposits. RBI had put it under prompt corrective action because its capital was below the minimum and its bad loans were high. It depended on a pending rescue merger with Indiabulls Housing, and on 30 September it fell amid reports of RBI curbs and doubts about that merger. Rivals: the 10 largest listed private banks.

DHFL (India), 1 October 2019. A housing-finance company funded by bank loans, debentures, commercial paper held largely by mutual funds, public deposits and securitisation. It had been in default on some obligations since June 2019. On 1 October it fell 20% on news of its exposure to the real-estate group HDIL and the failing PMC Bank. Rivals: the 10 largest listed housing-finance companies and NBFCs.

Adani Total Gas (India), 25 January 2023. A city-gas distributor (an Adani and TotalEnergies joint venture). On 24 January, after the Indian close, Hindenburg Research published a short-seller report on the Adani group alleging stock manipulation and accounting fraud. Rivals: other listed city-gas distributors (IGL, Gujarat Gas, Mahanagar Gas).

Cigna (US), 25 October 2002. A health insurer with a run-off reinsurance book. After a reinsurance charge on 18 October, it warned after the close on 24 October that third-quarter and full-year earnings would miss guidance. Rivals: S&P 500 firms in its current sub-industry, Health Care Services (CVS, DaVita, LabCorp, Quest).

UnumProvident (US), 10 March 2003. A disability and life insurer. A Moody's report questioned how its low-rated securities and claims affected its capital; there was no downgrade or missed payment that day. Rivals: S&P 500 life and health insurers (Aflac, Torchmark, MetLife, Principal, Prudential).

MBIA (US), 20 December 2007. A bond insurer whose business rests on its AAA rating. On 19 December, S&P moved its outlook to negative, and MBIA disclosed $8.1 billion of exposure to CDO-squared securities. The rating was not cut that day. Rivals: S&P 500 property-casualty insurers (Allstate, Cincinnati, Hartford, Progressive, Travelers).

Lincoln National (US), 17 November 2008. A life and annuity insurer. Hit by investment losses, it applied for TARP capital and to become a savings-and-loan holding company, while saying its capital was adequate. Many other firms also applied for TARP. Rivals: S&P 500 life and health insurers (Aflac, Torchmark, MetLife, Principal, Prudential).

Huntington Bancshares (US), 22 January 2009. A Midwest regional bank funded mainly by insured deposits. It reported a fourth-quarter 2008 loss on rising credit losses. Rivals: other S&P 500 regional banks (Fifth Third, KeyCorp, M&T, Regions).

ViacomCBS (US), 26 March 2021. A media group (CBS, Paramount). Banks sold large blocks of its shares for a client fund that had missed a margin call (Archegos Capital). Rivals: S&P 500 movies-and-entertainment firms (Live Nation, Netflix, Disney).
